topics.topic: Exact accepted IPv4 textual grammar, including digit alphabet, ranges, leading zeroes, signs, and whitespace
questions: Must each number use ASCII digits and lie from 0 through 255, and are leading zeroes in an IPv4 component accepted or refused?
What exact IPv4 grammar is accepted, including whether octets with leading zeroes, signs, whitespace, non-ASCII digits, or values outside 0–255 are refused?
Must IPv4 octets use the canonical ASCII form without leading zeroes, or are forms such as 127.000.000.001 accepted; and must each number explicitly be from 0 through 255?
Does “decimal digits” mean only ASCII 0–9, or every Unicode decimal-digit character accepted by the implementation language?

quotes:
An address is a host and a port, `host:port`:
   the host an IP address — an IPv6 one in brackets — and the port a whole
   number from 1 to 65535, the data provider's constants `LISTEN_PORT_MIN`
   and `LISTEN_PORT_MAX`, which the checking code imports (SPEC_STANDARD
   §15.3.1).

Written as text, an IPv4 host is four
   decimal numbers joined by dots and an IPv6 host the bracketed form any
   IPv6 text form names, each read into the address it names; the port is
   decimal digits without a leading zero.

A missing or malformed item fails the start; Registry applies no
   default to any item.
judgement.divergence: One implementation accepts leading-zero IPv4 components and Unicode decimal port digits after converting their numeric values; another accepts only ASCII canonical octets and ASCII port digits. The owner notices whether Registry starts.
judgement.why: The stated grammar fixes neither the digit alphabet nor leading-zero treatment, while those choices change whether a configured address is accepted.

Does “the same endpoint” include overlapping wildcard and specific-address binds on the same port, or only an identical host-and-port bind tuple?

quotes:
The two addresses have different ports, so that the two
   surfaces never share an endpoint, and Registry opens each listener for
   itself alone, never with an option that lets another active socket bind
   the same endpoint (no port sharing; rebinding a port a closed listener
   left is not sharing).
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats `0.0.0.0:8781` and `127.0.0.1:8781` as different endpoint tuples and permits their simultaneous bind when the platform allows it; another treats their traffic overlap as endpoint sharing and fails Registry's bind. The owner and callers notice the start result and which process receives traffic.
judgement.why: The text does not define whether “the same endpoint” is tuple equality or includes wildcard/specific-address overlap, nor does it identify behaviorally equivalent sharing options.

outcomes: Registry regards the host-and-port tuples as different, starts, and the platform may deliver traffic to either process.
Registry regards the wildcard bind as overlapping the existing endpoint and stops the start.

topics.topic: Failure behavior, diagnostic item, and ordering when exclusive or IPv6-only listening cannot be guaranteed
questions: If the operating system or listener API cannot guarantee exclusive binding or IPv6-only operation, must Registry fail the start, and which configured item must its diagnostic name?

Are enforcing IPv6-only operation and enforcing exclusive ownership part of this final listener-opening check, and if either cannot be established, which item is named and where does that failure fall in the stated first-failure order?

quotes:
4. **Open the listeners.** Last, `module:instance_lifecycle` opens the
   owner interface's listener and then, unless the start is owner-only, the
   service API's, each at its address in the loaded configuration — the
   deployment's, as R0-19 says (A17 rules 1, 2). One that cannot be opened stops
   the start with a diagnostic naming the surface: the listeners already
   opened are closed, then a store step 3 made new is removed, then the
   process ends with its one diagnostic, which names the surface that could
   not be opened and, when the new store could not be removed, that it was
   left; a close that fails is not named — the process's end releases the
   listener — and a store step 3 made new is removed by
   `capability:store.discard_new_store` — one it cannot remove is an empty
   store of the release's version, which the next start opens as any store
   (A17 rule 2). An existing store keeps its records as they were.
judgement.why: State 4 places both listener openings last, in owner-interface then service-API order, and says an unopenable conforming listener stops the start with a diagnostic naming the surface.

topics.topic: Whether explicitly configured IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses are valid
questions: Does this also forbid configuring an IPv4-mapped IPv6 host such as `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`, or does it only require an IPv6 listener to disable dual-stack acceptance of IPv4 connections?
Is an explicitly configured IPv4-mapped IPv6 address such as [::ffff:127.0.0.1] valid, or must it be refused because mapped IPv4 connections are forbidden?

quotes:
An IPv6 address is listened on for IPv6 alone, never
   for IPv4 connections mapped onto it.

Written as text, an IPv4 host is four
   decimal numbers joined by dots and an IPv6 host the bracketed form any
   IPv6 text form names, each read into the address it names; the port is
   decimal digits without a leading zero.

A missing or malformed item fails the start; Registry applies no
   default to any item.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` as a valid IPv6 literal and applies the IPv6-only socket rule; another treats the literal itself as the forbidden IPv4 mapping and refuses the configured address. The owner notices whether Registry starts.
judgement.why: The prohibition speaks about mapped IPv4 connections reaching an IPv6 listener but does not say whether an IPv4-mapped address literal is itself an accepted IPv6 host.

witness.initial: Registry is stopped with every item valid and the owner-interface address set to `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:8781`.
outcomes: Registry accepts the host as an IPv6 text form and attempts an IPv6-only bind.
Registry rejects the host as malformed because it denotes an IPv4-mapped address and stops the start.
witness.observer: The owner sees whether Registry starts.
basis:
An instance's configuration is set on its host, readable only by the owner and
the Registry process: on the VPS the compose environment file, on a local
instance the environment it is started with.

Registry checks the configuration when it starts and serves nothing until
   every check passes; a failed check stops the start with a diagnostic that
   names the failed item and never its value (R0-37).

topics.topic: Whether immediate rebinding after listener closure is required or merely permitted
questions: Is immediate rebinding of a recently closed listener required to succeed when the operating system can permit it, or is it merely allowed and a start may fail without a rebinding socket option?

quotes:
Registry opens each listener for

   the same endpoint (no port sharing; rebinding a port a closed listener
   left is not sharing).

last, the
   listener of each surface opened at its configured address (rule 1) — the
   owner interface's first, then the
   service API's unless the start is owner-only, one that cannot be opened
   failing the start and closing the one already opened.
judgement.divergence: One implementation enables a safe closed-listener rebinding facility and restarts immediately; another uses no such facility, cannot reopen a port retained by the operating system, and fails the start. The owner notices the restart result.
judgement.why: The text says post-close rebinding is not prohibited sharing, but does not require Registry to make such rebinding succeed when the platform offers a safe option.

events: The owner immediately starts Registry again with the same configured address.
outcomes: Registry uses the safe rebinding option, opens the listener and starts.
Registry uses no rebinding option, cannot open the listener and stops the start.
